title: Boeing
text: Today, Air France and KLM mark their 93rd and 107th anniversaries. Sometimes, the simplest images say it best: two aircraft, a KLM 787 shot from an Air France Boeing 787, flying in parallel, aligned, and often following the same path. Born in 1933 and 1919, and united since 2004, Air France and KLM have remained two distinct airlines with a shared trajectory. To all of our colleagues around the world: happy birthday, and thank you! You bring our brands, their history, values and legacy, to life every day. Joyeux anniversaire Air France ! Van Harte gefeliciteerd KLM Royal Dutch Airlines !

title: Ipsen
text: Vi presentiamo Carole. Lavora in Ipsen, ma il suo titolo professionale racconta solo una parte di ciò che è. Quando a sua madre è stata diagnosticata la malattia di Alzheimer, tutta la sua famiglia ne è stata profondamente coinvolta. Dietro l'assistente c'è una figlia. Una caregiver. Una collega. Nel corso degli anni, questa esperienza ha trasformato il loro rapporto in modi che Carole non avrebbe mai immaginato. Grazie, Carole, per aver condiviso la tua storia. Dietro ogni titolo professionale c'è una storia umana. Qual è la tua? Guarda il film completo. #ThisIsIpsen

title: Keiji Ogawa
text: Seven programs, same goal, completely different timelines I've been staring at this chart for a while now. Seven eVTOL programs. Same mission: build a certified aircraft people can actually buy. But look at how differently they're moving. Some companies locked in their design in 2015. Others were still changing it in 2023. Some went from program start to full-scale piloted testing in five years. Others took longer—or redesigned partway through. Some programs are still going. Some shut down. So, what's driving this? I don't think it's talent. These teams have some of the best engineers in the world. It's not just money, either. Many of these companies raised nine figures. There's something else. A decision made early—sometimes before the first prototype, sometimes before the full team is even hired. It looks purely technical at the time. But it creates a gap: Suppliers you don't have. Testing rigs you haven't built. Certification paths you've never walked. Processes that must scale faster than your team can learn. Some programs saw this gap coming and adjusted. Others discovered it years later, after burning through tens of millions of dollars. After 34 years in aerospace—including eVTOLs that flew, I've learned this: The most expensive mistakes aren't technical failures. They're mismatches between what you're trying to build and what your organization can actually handle. So, here's my question: If you're investing $50M in an eVTOL program, what do you ask before you write the check—beyond "Can this thing fly?" I’ve been tracking seven leading eVTOL programs for years — what pattern do you see when you look at their development timelines?
author: Keiji Ogawa
